3262.dq: The WIZ word consists of one stressed (or primarily stressed) syllable. ... There are a few words which function on the phrase level and have no stress.
3262.prule: One primary stress per word, lexically contrastive between the penultimate and the final syllable of the word stem (minimal pairs du1la3 'sin' / du1'la2 'large shawl', be12ga2 'gourd' / be2'ga3 'necklace'; 2016: beku 'perro' / bekú 'altar', sina / siná, inda / indá, ixi / ixí). Penult is the unmarked position ('in most cases... usually'); a lexical minority of ordinary native words (eagle, ravine, tail, altar, shawl, necklace, half, tasty...) has final stress instead. quantity-insensitive: long and glottalized ('broken') vowels occur only in the stressed syllable, so length follows stress rather than attracting it. A few phrase-level function words are stressless.
3262.srule: Secondary stress only in polymorphemic words (1 or 2 per word), placed by morphology on post-stem bound morphemes: all bound person markers except 3rd person common -ni3/-na2 (unstressed) and 1st plural inclusive ri?12 (a separate word with primary stress); the bound demonstratives -ni3 'here' / -na2 'there'; and the augment markers -do12 (diminutive) / -do3 (intensive). E.g. ru2'de3"lu2 'you-sg. are giving', 'zi1ta2"ni3 'this egg', 'i2za1"do12 'flower'. Secondarily stressed vowels are checked by lenis glottal closure utterance-finally; the plural clitic ka2- and location clitic -a1 are unstressed ('ru2xa3ka2na2 'they are carrying'). Not rhythmic/alternating.

Potts, James & Deibler 1974: phoneme chart lists High, Low, Rising; sec. 3 tone contrasts high vs low, low vs rising, high vs rising; p.7 'There has not been time to do an analysis of the tone system of Yaweyuha, and the conclusions contained herein and even the tones marked on examples are highly tentative. Rising tone has been noted on very few words, most of them monosyllabic'; 4.5 high tone has a down-glide allotone on the final syllable of final verbs; all tonemes have higher allotones at the beginning of a stream of speech, becoming progressively lower (downdrift); 6.2 proposes not to write tone (11 minimal pairs noted; the system 'appears to follow more the pattern of Gahuku'). Functional load of tone described as very low. On stress: Deibler 1976 p.4 'To date no analysis has been made of stress patterns on phonological words in Yaweyuha'; the word 'stress' does not occur in Potts et al. 1974; the OPD's 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' heading is followed only by the two-tone statement. 3265.dq: a shift of primary stress (a strictly phonetic feature) from the initial to the second syllable (*CV2) in Paman stems
3265.dloc: AL 8(2) pp.167-168 (Northern Paman initial reduction and stress shift; read)
3265.heavy: Not weight. The conditioning factor is the presence of an onset consonant: stress sits on the reflex of *CV2, i.e. on the first syllable preceded by a consonant (word-initial in C-initial words, second in V-initial words).
3265.dflt: not applicable (no weight condition); every word has at least one onsetful syllable, which carries the stress
3265.prule: Primary stress is non-contrastive ('a strictly phonetic feature') and falls on the syllable continuing Proto-Paman *CV2 (the second syllable of the proto-stem). Yinwum lost *C1 invariably and lost *V1 in some stems (mpi- 'give', lin 'mouth', ni- 'go', nti- 'spear', me- 'MM') but kept it in others (ayi 'vegetable food', iyi 'nose', uwu- 'far', ata 'crow'), so the surface locus is the first syllable of consonant-initial words and the second syllable of vowel-initial words: the first syllable that has an onset consonant. Hale states this synchronic formulation explicitly only for Linngithigh (p.179); for Yinwum it follows from the subgroup statement plus his Yinwum forms.
3265.srule: Not mentioned in Hale 1966 (AL 8(2) 162-197 read: the subgroup-level stress statement pp.167-168, the Yinwum passages pp.168-174 and the Linngithigh word-stress rule p.179 concern primary stress only; no secondary or rhythmic stress is mentioned).

3266.dq: We will describe the character of word stress in Yogad and then illustrate its operation. A minimal complete phonological utterance will have at least one most prominent syllable. The syllable with primary word stress is identified by the perception of its greater length and higher pitch. ... This secondary word stress will always precede the primary word stress ... 3266.dloc: Dictionary Introduction p. xx ('character of word stress': primary and secondary word stress) and p. xix (phonological word, exx. (46)-(47)).
3266.heavy: Not a placement factor. Phonetic note only (p. xxiii): closed syllables 'seem to be longer in the way that stressed open syllables are', so primary stress on a closed syllable is cued by higher pitch alone and secondary stress is inaudible (and unwritten) there.
3266.prule: Word stress is lexically contrastive and its position is not predictable: penult vs. final minimal pairs (lábat/labát, páyaw/payáw, áddu/addú, kúku/kukú, ámma/ammá; áttit/attít, taláttak/talatták). The authors state that 'position of stress remains highly variable' and mark stress on every headword where heard. Primary stress = greater length (open syllables) plus higher pitch.
3266.srule: Secondary stress exists, always precedes the primary, and is cued by length only (no pitch rise). It occurs in some polysyllabic words written with two stresses (binúkalú, barísibít, bóbidá) and when a lexical class of roots keeps its own stress before stressed -an/-uhn (túbug -> túbugán; none when stress shifts from a root-final vowel, tubúg -> tubugán); morphophonemic alternations may place it right before the primary. Its occurrence is not predictable ('complicated') and is written where heard; not written on closed syllables.

3268.dq: The tone domain is not the syllable nor the mora, but the word; one of the three distinctive melodies is mapped onto the word as a whole, regardless of its length. However, the actual tone-bearing unit is the syllable.

3268.heavy: Not a stress-weight condition. The source defines light (C)(G)V vs heavy (C)(G)VV, (C)(G)VN vs super-heavy (C)(G)VVN syllables (Sec. 2.4) only to state that the Falling tone's fall is realised on a heavy final syllable and not on a light one.
3268.prule: No stress rule: lexical three-way word-tone (N-pattern 'accent') system. Each simple noun carries one of three word melodies, High/A (final syllable high, preceding syllables high except the first: LH, LHH), Low/B (level low throughout) or Falling/C (like High but with a fall on a heavy final syllable; neutralised with High on a light final syllable unless a clitic adds weight; an unrealised fall downsteps the following word). The melody is a lexical property of the word, not a positional prominence.

tn.quote: Dunan has a three-way word-tone system for simple nouns. The tone domain is not the syllable nor the mora, but the word; one of the three distinctive melodies is mapped onto the word as a whole, regardless of its length. The Falling tone is similar to the High one, but the final syllable has a falling contour if it is heavy.

3270.heavy: Schooling 1992 (Gomen), pp.122-124: the heavy unit is 'a sequence of two contiguous vocalic nuclei, that is to say either a sequence of two syllables of Type 1 (V.V) or a sequence of a syllable of Type 2 followed by a syllable of Type 1 (CV.V)', long vowels included ('all vowel sequences, whether geminate vowels or heterogenous vowels, are to be interpreted as sequences of two vocalic phonemes' p.122; 'the VV sequence was exactly twice as long as a single vowel' p.123); Class 2 vowels /i, e, u, o/ 'may not function as the stressed nucleus of the phonological word if it is immediately preceded by another vowel in the same word' (p.122), so V+/a/ is not a heavy unit (/a/ 'can carry stress even if it is in second position in a sequence of two vowels', p.125). Bril & Galliot 2022 p.12: 'Un mot comportant une attaque et une voyelle longue comme kaa ‘récif coralien’ est mono-syllabique; en revanche, les suites vocaliques V.V sont fréquentes, elles sont hétéro-syllabiques, moraïques et forment des hiatus, comme ui [u.i] ‘souffler’' and the shift to the antepenult is 'pour des raisons de poids syllabique' (no further detail).
3270.dflt: penultimate syllable of the phonological word: 10 010 0010 00010 for 2-5 syllables (Schooling's phonological word is at most five syllables, sec. 5.2.1 p.123: stressed nucleus + 1-3 pre-nuclear syllables + one post-nuclear syllable; longer strings are compounds carrying two word stresses)
3270.prule: Stress on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word, in an analysis where every vowel is a syllable (long vowels and vowel sequences = V.V, sec. 5.1.2), with the restriction that a non-low vowel /i, e, u, o/ immediately preceded by another vowel cannot be the stressed nucleus (sec. 5.1.1), so in a (C)V.V sequence stress falls only on the first vowel: penult-final sequences keep penult stress (/'ui/, /'mpua/, /ha'xai/) but a sequence spanning antepenult+penult throws stress to the antepenult (/'haipo/ 'much', /'aiyu/ 'to inhabit'); the open vowel /a/ is exempt and takes penult stress as second vowel (/e'amwA/ 'where?', /ju'angA/ 'Yuanga'). Predictable, non-contrastive, demarcative; realised as extra expiratory force and lengthening of the stressed vowel. Bril & Galliot 2022 p.12, with long vowels as single syllables and V.V as moraic hiatus: 'Il se place sur l'avant-dernière syllabe du mot prosodique. Le pied est trochéique / ̄ ̆/, ('σs σw), et le calcul se fait à partir de la frontière droite du mot. L'accent peut se déplacer sur une syllabe antepenultième d'un mot prosodique pour des raisons de poids syllabique.' Read together: a right-edge bimoraic (moraic-trochee-like) window in which a VV unit (long vowel or V + non-low vowel) counts as heavy and is stressed on its first mora; neither source states the weight rule in full.
3270.srule: None: one stressed syllable per phonological word - 'In addition to the presence of one stressed syllable, a phonological word can be identified...'; 'The syllables which occur in the word margins are, by definition, unstressed.'

[...] This reveals that all underlying tones in Yukuna must surface, given the surface constraint for all phonological words to have at least one H syllable.

3272.prule: No positional or weight-based word stress. Word prosody is a restricted privative tone system (H vs. no tone; 'commonly labeled as pitch accent', a term the authors avoid): each root has exactly one syllable lexically specified for /H/ (spreads one syllable rightward) or /HL/ (non-spreading), bound to a root syllable or floating; affixes are toneless (except purposive /-ʧí/, /-ɾé/); unaffixed roots surface with at least one and at most two adjacent H syllables; floating tones dock on the first toneless TBU after the root; underlying /H/ vs /HL/ neutralised word-finally. Position of the H within the root is lexical and unpredictable.
3272.srule: Not mentioned in Lemus-Serrano, Allassonnière-Tang & Dediu 2021, Sec. 2 pp. 3-5 (word prosody analysed as privative H tone with no stress of any degree; a word's second surface H is spreading of one underlying /H/, not a secondary stress).

3273.prule: Tone language, not a stress-rule language: Yugh has four phonemic syllabic tones (features: high register, pharyngealisation, circumflex contour, abruptness), realised most fully on isolated monosyllables; in polysyllabic words a tone survives only in the stressed syllable, and 'stress' is defined as essentially the degree to which the tone is realised. Two further 'short-syllable accent types' are distinguished by where the F0 peak sits: on the first syllable (which 'gives the impression of dynamic word stress', e.g. dʌnyŋ 'knives') or on the last or penultimate syllable (e.g. kanča 'pipe'), with equal intensity on all syllables. No positional stress rule (fixed, weight-based or otherwise) is stated for the language.
3273.srule: Not mentioned in Werner 1997 (Языки мира sketch, §2.1.0–2.2.3, pp. 188–190 read in full): the sketch distinguishes only stressed (tone-bearing) vs. unstressed syllables; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described.

Four syllabic tones have been found in Yugh with the following characteristics: [table] Tones: First | Second | Third | Fourth -- High register + + + -; Pharyngealisation - + - +; Circumflex contour - + + +; Abruptness - + - -. 3278.prule: No positional or weight rule in either primary. Grefa Ushigua 2012 (native-author pedagogical grammar) classifies Sapara words into three stress classes, agudas (final), graves (penult) and esdrújulas (antepenult), lists 14-16 examples of each, and prescribes a written tilde on agudas and esdrújulas only; the lists contain the pair ikú 'siéntate' (aguda) vs iku 'huevo' (grave). 3280.dq: Kayan Lahta is a tonal language. There are 4 tones in Kayan Lahta and they are contrastive. ... (vii) Every syllable has tone.
3280.dloc: Ch. 2 Phonology: sec. 2.3 Tones, thesis p. 27; sec. 2.4.1 syllable-structure observation (vii), p. 30; sec. 2.4.2 Minor syllable, p. 31; sec. 7.3 Further research, p. 116. (pp. 42, 45, 46, 131).
3280.prule: No stress rule stated. The words stress, accent, prominence do not occur in the thesis.

3281.prule: Stress is expiratory (dynamic), not fixed, and non-contrastive; the placement rules differ by part of speech. 3286.loc: sec. 1 'Aperçu phonologique', B 'Les phonèmes supra-segmentaux', p. 436 (p. 432 of the Annales Aequatoria 13 (1992) volume scan)
3286.idn: The source describes Kisɛ́mbɔ́mbɔ (Kisémbombo), which the author calls 'un parler du kizimba (ou kibinja selon les locuteurs natifs)', i.e. one dialect of Zimba / Kibinja-Sud (Meeussen's 'kebinja du Sud', Guthrie D26; Atlas linguistique du Zaïre code 432), spoken at Lukamata, Kusu, Ngungwa, Kapuli-Unga, Misenga…
3286.tone: Two-tone system (H, L) with lexical minimal pairs; the mora is the tone-bearing unit ('chaque more d'une voyelle longue porte un ton'); contour tones not established as contrastive; vowel length non-distinctive. The article never uses accent/stress/intensité/tonique/pénultième/proéminence (a full-text search of the article range: no hits), nor does the 1994 sequel 'Les formes pronominales en kisémbómbo' (Annales Aequatoria 15: 269-281: no hits). So the source is a tone description that does not discuss stress, not a denial of stress.
